name: OMK 2A Heme — Summative 3 Objective Review · Board-Style Set 5 (Hard)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is gravida 2, para 1, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the office for a routine prenatal visit. She is RhD-negative; her first child is RhD-positive and she received no RhD immune globulin after that delivery. She feels well and reports normal fetal movement. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a fundal height appropriate for dates. The obstetrician wishes to determine whether this pregnancy is at risk of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. Which of the following tests, and on which specimen, will answer that question?
choices: A. Direct antiglobulin test on the mother's erythrocytes
B. Direct antiglobulin test on the mother's plasma
C. Indirect antiglobulin test on the mother's plasma
D. Indirect antiglobulin test performed on paternal erythrocytes
E. Osmotic fragility testing of the mother's erythrocytes
questions.explanation: The two antiglobulin tests ask different questions, and choosing between them is a matter of deciding whose cells are at risk. The DIRECT test asks: are the patient's OWN erythrocytes already coated with antibody? It is the test you run on a patient who is hemolysing now — the newborn after delivery, or a suspected autoimmune or transfusion-related hemolysis. The INDIRECT test asks: does the patient's PLASMA contain antibody capable of binding other people's cells? That is exactly the question here. The mother's own erythrocytes are RhD-negative and are in no danger; what matters is whether she was sensitized by her first RhD-positive infant and now carries circulating anti-D that can cross the placenta and destroy FETAL cells. The indirect antiglobulin test is the routine antibody screen, and if anti-D is detected it is titred and the pregnancy monitored — classically with middle cerebral artery Doppler peak systolic velocity to detect fetal anemia. This is also why RhD immune globulin, which she did not receive, is given to prevent sensitization in the first place.

wrongExplanations.0: A direct antiglobulin test on the MOTHER would ask whether her own erythrocytes are antibody-coated. They are RhD-negative, so anti-D has nothing on them to bind — the test would be negative and would say nothing about fetal risk. This test becomes useful on the INFANT's cells after delivery.
wrongExplanations.1: A direct antiglobulin test is performed on erythrocytes, not on plasma — the whole point is to detect antibody already attached to cells. Running it on plasma is not a valid procedure, which makes this option a test of whether the two assays are genuinely understood.
wrongExplanations.3: Paternal typing can establish whether the fetus could be RhD-positive at all, and is sometimes used, but an antiglobulin test performed on paternal cells is not the assay. The clinically decisive question is whether the MOTHER'S PLASMA contains the antibody, and cell-free fetal DNA can now determine fetal RhD type directly.
wrongExplanations.4: Osmotic fragility testing evaluates erythrocyte membrane surface-to-volume ratio and is used for hereditary SPHEROCYTOSIS. It has no role in detecting alloantibody and would tell nothing about this pregnancy.

questions.eli5: One version of this test asks whether a person's own red cells are already coated with antibody; the other asks whether their liquid blood contains antibody that could attack someone else's cells. Her own cells are fine — the worry is her plasma reaching the baby. So the second version, run on her plasma, is the one that answers it.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia is admitted for induction chemotherapy. He is profoundly neutropenic and is expected to require multiple transfusions. His sister, who is a partial human leukocyte antigen match, asks to donate blood directly for him, saying she would prefer he receive her blood rather than that of a stranger. The transfusion service agrees to prepare her unit. Which of the following modifications to the donated unit is most important to prevent a fatal complication?
choices: A. Gamma irradiation of the unit
B. Leukocyte reduction of the unit
C. Selection of a cytomegalovirus-seronegative donor
D. Volume reduction of the unit
E. Washing the unit to remove residual plasma
questions.explanation: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease occurs when viable donor T lymphocytes engraft in a recipient who cannot reject them, then attack the recipient's tissues. It appears 1 to 6 weeks later with pancytopenia, rash, diarrhea, and liver dysfunction, and it is USUALLY FATAL — there is no effective treatment, so prevention is the entire management. Gamma irradiation of the unit cross-links donor lymphocyte DNA so those cells cannot proliferate, and it is the ONLY intervention that prevents it. The counterintuitive part is why a relative is MORE dangerous than a stranger. A partially HLA-matched donor's lymphocytes can look sufficiently 'self' that the recipient's immune system does not reject them, while remaining different enough to attack the recipient — so directed donation from family members carries a HIGHER risk, and irradiation is mandatory for related-donor units even in immunocompetent recipients. It is also required for the severely immunocompromised, as this patient will be.

wrongExplanations.1: Leukocyte reduction removes the great majority of white cells and is standard of care for essentially every unit in the United States. It prevents FEBRILE NONHEMOLYTIC reactions and reduces HLA alloimmunization and cytomegalovirus transmission — but it does NOT reliably eliminate graft-versus-host disease, because the residual lymphocytes are still enough to engraft.
wrongExplanations.2: A cytomegalovirus-seronegative donor reduces the risk of transmitting cytomegalovirus to a severely immunocompromised recipient, and is a legitimate consideration. It has no bearing on whether donor lymphocytes engraft and attack his tissues.
wrongExplanations.3: Volume reduction lessens the risk of transfusion-associated circulatory overload in patients who cannot tolerate fluid load, such as small children or those in heart failure. It does not remove or inactivate donor lymphocytes.
wrongExplanations.4: Washing removes residual plasma and is the answer for a patient with IgA deficiency and anti-IgA antibodies at risk of ANAPHYLAXIS, or for repeated severe allergic reactions. It does not address the cellular component that causes graft-versus-host disease.

questions.eli5: Living white cells in donated blood can take root in a patient whose immune system is too weak to reject them, then attack his body — and there is no cure once it starts. Radiation of the bag stops those cells from multiplying. Oddly, blood from a relative is riskier than from a stranger, because a partial match is exactly what slips past the immune system.

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She feels entirely well and has had no bleeding, bruising, petechiae, or recent illness. She takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities, and there is no purpura, no lymphadenopathy, and no splenomegaly. A complete blood count drawn into an EDTA tube shows:

    Hemoglobin              13.6 g/dL
    Leukocyte count         6,400/mm3
    Platelet count          21,000/mm3

She is called back urgently. A repeat sample, again drawn into EDTA, shows a platelet count of 24,000/mm3. Review of the peripheral blood smear shows large aggregates of platelets at the feather edge and along the sides of the film; individual platelets appear normal in size and granularity, and erythrocytes and leukocytes are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: A. Administration of intravenous immune globulin to raise the platelet count
B. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy to assess megakaryocyte number
C. Repeat the complete blood count on a specimen collected in sodium citrate
D. Testing for antiplatelet glycoprotein-specific antibodies
E. Transfusion of platelets for the reported count
questions.explanation: This is EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia, and the clue is the mismatch between a dangerously low number and a completely well patient with a normal examination. Automated analyzers count particles by size. Platelet CLUMPS are too large to be counted as platelets, so the analyzer simply misses them and reports a falsely LOW count — the same size-based error that makes microcytes, schistocytes, and leukocyte fragments get counted AS platelets and falsely raise the count in the other direction. Here the cause is an antibody that agglutinates platelets only in the presence of EDTA, the anticoagulant in the standard purple-top tube. It is an in vitro artefact with no clinical consequence whatsoever. The fix is to redraw into a different anticoagulant — sodium citrate — or to use the analyzer's fluorescent platelet channel, which identifies platelets by nucleic acid content rather than by size. Always reconcile the number with the patient: a genuine count of 21,000/mm3 would usually produce petechiae or mucosal bleeding, and she has none.

wrongExplanations.0: Intravenous immune globulin treats immune thrombocytopenic purpura, which requires a TRUE low platelet count. Treating an artefact would expose her to the costs and risks of therapy for a disease she does not have.
wrongExplanations.1: Marrow examination would be appropriate for an unexplained genuine thrombocytopenia, particularly with other cytopenias or abnormal cells. Her other lines are normal and the smear explains the number, so a marrow biopsy would be an invasive answer to a question the slide has already settled.
wrongExplanations.3: Antiplatelet antibody testing has poor sensitivity and specificity and is not used to diagnose immune thrombocytopenic purpura, which remains a clinical diagnosis of exclusion. It would also be pursuing a real disease that this patient does not have.
wrongExplanations.4: Platelet transfusion for a count of 21,000/mm3 in a non-bleeding patient would be questionable even if the count were real — the hypoproliferative threshold is 10,000/mm3. Transfusing for an artefact exposes her to alloimmunization and transfusion reactions for no benefit at all.

questions.eli5: Her platelets clumped together inside the collection tube because of the chemical used to stop the blood clotting. The machine counts by size, so clumps are too big to register as platelets and it reported far too few. She has no bruising or bleeding, which is the giveaway — redrawing into a different tube gives the real number.

questions.stem:
A 21-year-old woman is referred for evaluation of a lifelong mild anemia. Her father and paternal grandmother both underwent splenectomy in early adulthood for anemia, and her father has had gallstones. She has had intermittent scleral icterus during febrile illnesses but has never required transfusion. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild scleral icterus and a spleen palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  10.8 g/dL
    Hematocrit                                  32%
    Mean corpuscular volume                     84 μm3
    Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration   37.2 g/dL (N=32–36)
    Reticulocyte count                          6.4%
    Total bilirubin                             2.6 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin                            0.3 mg/dL

A peripheral blood smear read from the monolayer shows numerous small, densely staining erythrocytes lacking central pallor. A direct antiglobulin test is NEGATIVE. Which of the following best explains why the osmotic fragility test is abnormal in this disorder?
choices: A. Hemoglobin within the cell precipitates when the cell is placed in hypotonic saline
B. The cell has reduced surface area relative to its volume, so it can swell very little before lysing
C. The cell is coated with antibody, which weakens the membrane on exposure to hypotonic saline
D. The cell lacks the enzymes needed to generate the energy required to maintain its shape
E. The cell membrane is abnormally permeable to sodium and water
questions.explanation: The osmotic fragility test is old-fashioned, but its logic IS the disease. Erythrocytes are placed in progressively hypotonic saline; water enters and the cell swells. A normal biconcave disc carries SPARE MEMBRANE relative to its volume, so it can take on a great deal of water and round up into a sphere before the membrane finally gives way. A spherocyte is ALREADY a sphere — the defective membrane skeleton (mutations in ANK1, SPTB, or SLC4A1, affecting ankyrin, spectrin, and band 3) has allowed the spleen to strip membrane away, so surface area is reduced relative to volume and there is no spare capacity. It therefore lyses at a much higher saline concentration than a normal cell — increased fragility. The same geometry explains the high MEAN CORPUSCULAR HEMOGLOBIN CONCENTRATION of 37.2 g/dL: the cell is smaller for the hemoglobin it contains. Hereditary spherocytosis is the ONE genuine exception to the rule that a value above about 36 to 37 g/dL is an artefact. The negative direct antiglobulin test is what excludes autoimmune hemolysis, which produces an identical smear.

wrongExplanations.0: Hemoglobin precipitation on oxidative stress produces HEINZ BODIES and bite cells, as in G6PD deficiency. It is a chemical injury to hemoglobin, not a geometric limitation of the membrane, and it is not what the osmotic fragility test measures.
wrongExplanations.2: Antibody coating does produce spherocytes, by the same splenic membrane-stripping mechanism, and such cells ARE osmotically fragile. But that is autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is excluded here by the NEGATIVE direct antiglobulin test — the single result that separates the two disorders.
wrongExplanations.3: An enzyme deficiency describes pyruvate kinase or G6PD deficiency, in which the cell cannot generate adenosine triphosphate or reducing power. Those are nonspherocytic hemolytic anemias — the membrane skeleton itself is structurally normal and osmotic fragility is not characteristically increased.
wrongExplanations.4: Abnormal cation permeability describes hereditary STOMATOCYTOSIS and related disorders, in which sodium and water leak into the cell. Those cells show a slit-like central pallor rather than none at all, and the mechanism is transport rather than deficient surface area.

questions.eli5: A normal red cell is a flattened disc with plenty of slack membrane, so it can soak up water and puff into a ball before bursting. Hers have already lost that slack and are balls to begin with, so even a little water bursts them. That is what the test measures, and it is why the cells look small and dark on the slide.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with homozygous sickle cell disease is seen in clinic for routine follow-up. He has had three vaso-occlusive pain crises requiring hospitalization in the past year and one episode of acute chest syndrome. He takes penicillin prophylaxis and folic acid, and his vaccinations are current. He is asymptomatic today. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and no acute findings. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 7.8 g/dL, a reticulocyte count of 9.2%, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing 86% hemoglobin S, 4% hemoglobin F, and 6% hemoglobin A2. Hydroxyurea is recommended. Which of the following best describes how this drug reduces his risk of further crises?
choices: A. It chelates iron accumulated from chronic hemolysis, reducing oxidative membrane damage
B. It increases hemoglobin F, which does not participate in hemoglobin S polymerization
C. It inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, killing the sickled erythrocytes preferentially
D. It raises erythrocyte 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve
E. It suppresses the marrow, lowering the total number of sickle cells produced
questions.explanation: Sickling is a POLYMERIZATION problem: deoxygenated hemoglobin S polymerizes into rigid fibers that deform the cell. Every effective therapy attacks that polymer, and they do so from different directions. Hydroxyurea induces hemoglobin F (alpha-2 gamma-2), and hemoglobin F polymerizes POORLY with hemoglobin S — so raising it DILUTES the polymer and raises the threshold of deoxygenation at which sickling begins. His hemoglobin F is only 4%, leaving substantial room. The same logic explains the alternatives: transfusion adds hemoglobin A, achieving the same dilution from the other direction; intravenous fluids lower the intracellular hemoglobin concentration; supplemental oxygen keeps hemoglobin in the oxygenated conformation, which does not polymerize; and gene therapy either switches hemoglobin F back on or inserts a working beta gene. The anchoring number is that keeping hemoglobin S below 30% significantly decreases stroke risk in randomized trials — and the reason severe episodes need EXCHANGE rather than simple transfusion is arithmetic: you cannot dilute 86% hemoglobin S below 30% by adding blood without making the patient dangerously polycythemic.

wrongExplanations.0: Iron chelation with deferasirox or deferoxamine is important in a CHRONICALLY TRANSFUSED patient who has accumulated iron, but it does nothing to prevent sickling and is not hydroxyurea's mechanism. This patient is not transfusion-dependent.
wrongExplanations.2: Hydroxyurea does inhibit ribonucleotide reductase — that is its cytotoxic action, and the reason it is also used for cytoreduction in myeloproliferative neoplasms. But that is not how it helps in sickle cell disease, and it does not selectively kill sickled cells. Naming a true property that is the wrong explanation is the trap here.
wrongExplanations.3: Raising 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shifts the curve RIGHT, promoting oxygen unloading and therefore MORE deoxygenated hemoglobin S — which would worsen sickling, not prevent it. Hemoglobin F binds 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate poorly, giving it higher oxygen affinity.
wrongExplanations.4: Myelosuppression is a dose-limiting ADVERSE EFFECT of hydroxyurea requiring blood count monitoring, not its therapeutic mechanism. Simply making fewer erythrocytes would worsen an already anemic patient.

questions.eli5: Sickling happens when one type of hemoglobin links up into stiff rods inside the cell. This drug switches back on the fetal version of hemoglobin, which refuses to join those rods. More of the non-joining kind means the rods form less easily, so the cells keep their shape.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman receiving induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia develops a single temperature of 38.4°C (101.1°F) on day 9. She feels mildly fatigued but has no cough, dysuria, diarrhea, abdominal pain, or rash. Her pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no mucositis, a clean and non-erythematous tunnelled catheter exit site, clear lung fields, a soft nontender abdomen, and no perianal tenderness. A chest x-ray shows no infiltrate. Laboratory studies show:

    Leukocyte count             400/mm3
      Segmented neutrophils     12%
      Band forms                2%
    Hemoglobin                  8.9 g/dL
    Platelet count              34,000/mm3

Urinalysis is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Administration of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics after obtaining cultures
B. Administration of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor without antibiotics
C. Observation with repeat temperature measurement in 4 hours and reassessment
D. Transfusion of granulocytes from a directed donor
E. Withholding antibiotics until a source of infection has been identified on imaging
questions.explanation: Her absolute neutrophil count is 400 x (12 + 2)/100 = 56/mm3 — profoundly neutropenic. Below 200/mm3 there is essentially NO INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE, and that single fact governs the entire encounter. With no neutrophils there is nothing to generate pus, erythema, an infiltrate on chest film, or pyuria on urinalysis, so a reassuringly normal examination and normal imaging CANNOT exclude infection — they are exactly what you expect in a patient who cannot mount a response. Fever may therefore be the only sign an infection ever produces, and untreated neutropenic sepsis progresses to shock within hours. Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency: obtain blood cultures from the catheter and a peripheral site, then give empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics with antipseudomonal coverage IMMEDIATELY, ideally within an hour, without waiting for a source or for results. Note the parallel with the asplenic patient, where the same logic and the same urgency apply.

wrongExplanations.1: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor shortens the duration of neutropenia and has a role as prophylaxis or adjunct, but it takes days to raise the neutrophil count. Giving it INSTEAD of antibiotics leaves the patient unprotected through the hours that determine the outcome.
wrongExplanations.2: Observation is the error this scenario is built to catch. A single temperature of 38.3°C or higher in a neutropenic patient meets the definition of febrile neutropenia, and the absence of localizing findings is expected rather than reassuring.
wrongExplanations.3: Granulocyte transfusion is an investigational and rarely used measure, considered only for documented infection refractory to maximal antimicrobial therapy in prolonged neutropenia. It is never the initial step.
wrongExplanations.4: Waiting for a source inverts the logic of the disease. A neutropenic patient often NEVER develops a localizing sign, and in roughly half of cases no source is ever identified — which is precisely why therapy is empiric.

questions.eli5: Chemotherapy has wiped out the cells that create redness, swelling, and pus, so an infection can be raging with nothing to see on examination or on the x-ray. A fever may be the only clue he gets. Cultures are drawn and antibiotics started within the hour, before anyone knows where the infection is.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man comes to the office because of a 4-month history of fatigue, lower back pain, and constipation. He has had no fever or night sweats. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor and tenderness over the lower thoracic vertebrae. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  8.9 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  27%
    Serum calcium               12.4 mg/dL
    Serum creatinine            3.1 mg/dL (baseline 0.9)
    Serum total protein         9.6 g/dL
    Serum albumin               3.2 g/dL

Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal IgG kappa spike of 2.4 g/dL. Serum free light chain assay shows a markedly elevated kappa concentration with a kappa-to-lambda ratio of 180. Bone marrow biopsy shows 48% clonal plasma cells. A skeletal survey shows multiple lytic lesions in the vertebrae and skull. Urinalysis by dipstick shows trace protein, but a 24-hour urine collection contains 4.2 g of protein. Which of the following best explains this patient's renal failure?
choices: A. Amyloid deposition within glomerular capillary walls
B. Deposition of monoclonal IgG immune complexes in the mesangium
C. Hypercalcemia-induced afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction alone
D. Precipitation of filtered free light chains within the renal tubules
E. Tumor lysis from spontaneous plasma cell turnover
questions.explanation: Antibodies are built from a heavy chain and a light chain, and a myeloma clone often produces light chains in vast excess. Because light chains are SMALL they are freely filtered by the glomerulus, reach the tubule in high concentration, and precipitate there with Tamm-Horsfall protein to form obstructing casts — light chain cast nephropathy, or myeloma kidney. This is why free light chains are measured SEPARATELY from the electrophoresis: a patient can have devastating light chain disease with an unimpressive monoclonal spike, and the kidney is the organ that pays. The urine findings prove the mechanism: a dipstick detects mainly ALBUMIN and reads only trace, while a 24-hour collection shows 4.2 g — the discrepancy means the protein being lost is not albumin but filtered light chains (Bence Jones protein). His picture is the full CRAB tetrad that converts a watched precursor state into treated myeloma: hyperCalcemia at 12.4 mg/dL, Renal failure, Anemia at 8.9 g/dL, and Bone lesions. Management includes vigorous hydration, treating the hypercalcemia, avoiding nephrotoxins and contrast, and starting anti-myeloma therapy promptly.

wrongExplanations.0: AL amyloidosis does arise from deposited light chains and is a genuine complication of plasma cell disorders. But glomerular amyloid causes NEPHROTIC-range ALBUMINURIA, which a dipstick detects readily — the opposite of the dipstick-negative, collection-positive pattern described here. Diagnosis requires Congo red staining with apple-green birefringence.
wrongExplanations.1: Immune complex deposition in the mesangium describes glomerulonephritis, which presents with hematuria, dysmorphic erythrocytes, and red cell casts. Myeloma light chains injure the TUBULES rather than depositing as complexes in the glomerulus.
wrongExplanations.2: Hypercalcemia genuinely contributes — it causes vasoconstriction, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with volume depletion, and nephrocalcinosis, and it must be treated. But the word 'alone' is what makes this wrong: it would not produce 4.2 g of non-albumin proteinuria, which points squarely at filtered light chains.
wrongExplanations.4: Tumor lysis syndrome occurs after treatment of a bulky, RAPIDLY DIVIDING tumor and produces high potassium, high phosphate, high urate, and LOW calcium. Myeloma is a slowly proliferating plasma cell neoplasm, he has not been treated, and his calcium is HIGH, not low.

questions.eli5: His plasma cells are churning out small antibody fragments that slip easily through the kidney's filter and then clog the drainage tubes downstream. The urine dipstick only really detects a different protein, which is why it looked almost normal while a full-day collection found grams of protein. That mismatch is the fingerprint.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with a 9-year history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia, previously managed with observation alone, comes to the office because of a rapidly enlarging mass in the left neck that has grown over 5 weeks. He has had drenching night sweats and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss over the same period. Previously his lymphadenopathy had been stable and nontender for years. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 126/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a firm, fixed 7-cm left cervical mass; other nodal areas are unchanged. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 9.6 g/dL, a lymphocyte count of 62,000/mm3, a platelet count of 88,000/mm3, and a lactate dehydrogenase of 1,180 U/L (previously 190 U/L). Excisional biopsy of the mass shows sheets of large lymphoid cells with vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli, and a proliferation index of 85%. Which of the following best explains these findings?
choices: A. Coexistent tuberculous lymphadenitis
B. Development of autoimmune hemolytic anemia
C. Progression to accelerated-phase chronic myeloid leukemia
D. Reactive lymphadenopathy from an intercurrent viral infection
E. Transformation to a high-grade large B-cell lymphoma
questions.explanation: This is Richter transformation — the evolution of an indolent chronic lymphocytic leukemia into an aggressive large B-cell lymphoma, occurring in roughly 5% to 10% of patients. Every feature signals the change in TEMPO that defines it: a single node growing rapidly and asymmetrically while the others stay stable, new B symptoms, and a lactate dehydrogenase that has risen sixfold. The biopsy confirms it with sheets of LARGE cells and a proliferation index of 85%, in place of the small mature-appearing lymphocytes with coarse chromatin that characterize chronic lymphocytic leukemia. This is also a clean illustration of the differentiation rule: less differentiated means more aggressive, which inverts curability — the indolent disease he had for 9 years was essentially incurable but compatible with long survival, while this aggressive one is potentially curable yet lethal within months untreated. Note the diagnostic principle as well: an EXCISIONAL biopsy of the discordant node was required, because a fine-needle aspirate could easily have sampled residual chronic lymphocytic leukemia and missed the transformation.

wrongExplanations.0: Tuberculous lymphadenitis can produce a firm, matted mass with fever, sweats, and weight loss in an immunocompromised patient, making it a real clinical consideration. It is excluded by the biopsy, which shows sheets of monomorphic large lymphoid cells rather than caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli.
wrongExplanations.1: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is a genuine and common complication of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and could explain his falling hemoglobin. It would show a positive direct antiglobulin test, spherocytes, reticulocytosis, and a raised bilirubin — and crucially it would not produce a rapidly enlarging nodal mass full of large cells.
wrongExplanations.2: Accelerated-phase chronic MYELOID leukemia is the wrong lineage entirely. It arises from BCR-ABL1-positive myeloid disease and is defined by 20% or more basophils, with blasts of 20% or more marking blast phase. His disease is a mature B-cell neoplasm.
wrongExplanations.3: Reactive lymphadenopathy follows an identifiable trigger, is soft, tender, and mobile, regresses over weeks, and is confined to the drainage territory of the trigger. His node is firm, fixed, progressive over 5 weeks, and histologically monomorphic and malignant.

questions.eli5: He had a slow-growing blood cancer that was safe to simply watch for nine years. One lymph node then started growing fast while the others stayed put, with fevers and weight loss — a change of pace that means the disease has switched into an aggressive form. Removing the whole node showed large, fast-dividing cells instead of the small quiet ones.

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old woman with osteosarcoma receives high-dose methotrexate. Her renal function was normal before the infusion. Thirty-six hours later she has severe oral ulceration and is unable to swallow. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F), pulse is 108/min, and blood pressure is 104/64 mm Hg. Physical examination shows confluent ulceration of the buccal and labial mucosa and a desquamating erythematous rash over the trunk. Laboratory studies show:

    Leukocyte count             1,100/mm3
    Platelet count              42,000/mm3
    Serum creatinine            2.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.8)
    Serum methotrexate          Markedly elevated for the time since infusion

Review of the chart shows that the scheduled rescue agent was inadvertently omitted, and that she had been started on ibuprofen for bone pain 2 days before the infusion. Which of the following agents should have been administered, and by what mechanism does it act?
choices: A. Dexrazoxane, which chelates intracellular iron and thereby prevents free radical generation
B. Glucarpidase, which converts methotrexate into an active intracellular polyglutamate
C. Leucovorin, which competitively displaces methotrexate from dihydrofolate reductase
D. Leucovorin, which supplies reduced folate downstream of the enzyme that methotrexate blocks
E. Mesna, which binds the urotoxic metabolite acrolein within the bladder
questions.explanation: Methotrexate inhibits DIHYDROFOLATE REDUCTASE, so the cell cannot regenerate tetrahydrofolate and cannot make thymidylate or purines — DNA synthesis stops, and the fastest-dividing tissues suffer first: oral and gastrointestinal mucosa and marrow. Leucovorin (folinic acid) is ALREADY REDUCED folate. It therefore enters the pathway DOWNSTREAM of the blocked enzyme, bypassing the block entirely and rescuing normal cells without requiring the enzyme to be freed. That distinction matters — it is a bypass, not a competitive displacement. Two things worsened her exposure: the omitted rescue, and the ibuprofen, since nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs reduce renal methotrexate clearance and can precipitate exactly this toxicity. The final caution is the one most often missed: leucovorin cuts both ways. It is a RESCUE agent for methotrexate but an ENHANCER for 5-fluorouracil, stabilizing that drug's inhibition of thymidylate synthase. Same molecule, opposite intent — never assume leucovorin means antidote.

wrongExplanations.0: Dexrazoxane chelates intracellular iron so it cannot react with superoxide and hydrogen peroxide to generate free radicals, protecting cardiac muscle. It is the cardioprotectant paired with ANTHRACYCLINES and has no role in folate metabolism.
wrongExplanations.1: Glucarpidase is a real and useful drug in methotrexate toxicity with renal impairment, but the mechanism stated is wrong and inverted: it is a bacterial enzyme that CLEAVES methotrexate into inactive metabolites, providing an alternative clearance route. It does not create an active polyglutamate — intracellular polyglutamation is what makes methotrexate MORE potent and retained.
wrongExplanations.2: This names the correct drug with the wrong mechanism, and is the strongest distractor. Leucovorin does not compete with methotrexate for dihydrofolate reductase or displace it from the enzyme; it enters the pathway beyond the blockade as a already-reduced folate.
wrongExplanations.4: Mesna binds acrolein, the urotoxic metabolite of CYCLOPHOSPHAMIDE and ifosfamide, preventing hemorrhagic cystitis. It is a bladder protectant and has nothing to do with folate or mucositis.

questions.eli5: The chemotherapy blocks an enzyme that makes the usable form of folate, and cells cannot build DNA without it — so the mouth lining and bone marrow break down first. The rescue drug is folate that has already been converted, so it simply steps in past the blocked enzyme. It was left out, and a painkiller she took slowed the drug's removal by the kidneys.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer has been receiving trastuzumab with a taxane for 7 months, following four cycles of doxorubicin-based chemotherapy completed 9 months ago. She comes to the office because of a 3-week history of exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and ankle swelling. She does not smoke and has no history of hypertension or coronary disease. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows jugular venous distention, an S3 gallop, bibasilar crackles, and bilateral pitting ankle edema. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 34%, reduced from 62% before treatment, with global hypokinesis. Which of the following best explains this adverse effect?
choices: A. Free radical generation from iron complexed with the anthracycline
B. Immune-mediated myocarditis from checkpoint blockade
C. Inhibition of a receptor that is also expressed on normal cardiomyocytes
D. Microtubule stabilization impairing cardiac contractile protein turnover
E. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy precipitated by the stress of illness
questions.explanation: Predict the toxicity from the CLASS, and for targeted agents the rule is that toxicity appears WHEREVER THE TARGET IS NORMALLY EXPRESSED. HER2 (ERBB2) is not confined to tumor — it is expressed on normal cardiomyocytes, where HER2 signalling supports survival and the response to stress. Blocking it with trastuzumab impairs that pathway and produces a cardiomyopathy that is typically DOSE-INDEPENDENT and largely REVERSIBLE on stopping the drug, which is why ejection fraction is monitored serially throughout treatment. This is the same logic that explains the acne-like rash and diarrhea of EGFR inhibitors, since EGFR is expressed in skin and gut. Her prior anthracycline is genuinely relevant — the two toxicities are additive, and prior anthracycline exposure is a recognized risk factor for trastuzumab cardiotoxicity — but anthracycline injury is a different mechanism with a different profile.

wrongExplanations.0: This is the anthracycline mechanism: doxorubicin complexes with intracellular iron and generates free radicals that damage cardiac myocytes, giving a CUMULATIVE, DOSE-DEPENDENT, and largely IRREVERSIBLE cardiomyopathy (and it is why dexrazoxane, an iron chelator, is cardioprotective). Her anthracycline finished 9 months ago after only four cycles, and the temporal relationship points to the current drug.
wrongExplanations.1: Immune-mediated myocarditis is a recognized and dangerous complication of CHECKPOINT INHIBITORS such as pembrolizumab and ipilimumab, where removing an immune brake causes autoimmunity in any organ. Trastuzumab is a targeted antibody against a growth factor receptor, not a checkpoint inhibitor, and she is not receiving one.
wrongExplanations.3: Taxanes act by stabilizing microtubules and preventing their disassembly, and their characteristic dose-limiting toxicity is peripheral NEUROPATHY, not cardiomyopathy. Microtubule effects do not produce global left ventricular hypokinesis.
wrongExplanations.4: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a stress-induced condition with characteristic apical ballooning and basal sparing, typically after an acute emotional or physical trigger. Her echocardiogram shows GLOBAL hypokinesis developing over months during treatment with a drug known to cause exactly this.

questions.eli5: The drug works by blocking a growth signal that her tumor depends on. The problem is that healthy heart muscle uses the same signal to stay resilient, so blocking it everywhere weakens the heart too. That is why her heart function is checked regularly during treatment — and it usually recovers once the drug is stopped.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with relapsed precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia receives an infusion of autologous chimeric antigen receptor T cells directed against CD19. On day 4 he develops fever to 40.1°C (104.2°F), rigors, and hypotension. His pulse is 132/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 76/44 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen saturation of 89% on 4 L/min by nasal cannula. Physical examination shows warm extremities and bibasilar crackles. Blood and urine cultures obtained 24 hours ago show no growth, and a chest x-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates without consolidation. Laboratory studies show a C-reactive protein of 28 mg/dL, a ferritin of 12,400 ng/mL, and a markedly elevated interleukin-6 concentration. He remains hypotensive after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: A. Intravenous immune globulin
B. Plasma exchange
C. Rituximab
D. Therapeutic heparin infusion
E. Tocilizumab
questions.explanation: This is CYTOKINE RELEASE SYNDROME, the signature toxicity of therapies that force T cells onto tumor cells — chimeric antigen receptor T cells and the bispecific T-cell engagers, which bridge a tumor antigen to CD3 on a passing T lymphocyte (blinatumomab against CD19, teclistamab against BCMA, mosunetuzumab and glofitamab against CD20). Massive T-cell activation releases a flood of cytokines, of which INTERLEUKIN-6 is the central mediator, producing high fever, distributive shock with warm extremities, hypoxemia, and a hyperinflammatory laboratory picture with a very high ferritin and C-reactive protein. It typically begins within the first week, distinguishing it from the other characteristic toxicity of these agents, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome. The treatment is TOCILIZUMAB, a monoclonal antibody against the interleukin-6 receptor, which reverses the syndrome without killing the engineered T cells; corticosteroids are added for severe or refractory cases. Sepsis must be treated empirically in parallel, since the presentations are indistinguishable and the patient is neutropenic — but negative cultures with a ferritin of 12,400 ng/mL point firmly here.

wrongExplanations.0: Intravenous immune globulin is given to these patients for the B-cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia that follow CD19-directed therapy, since the treatment destroys normal B cells along with the tumor. That is a later, chronic consequence, and it does nothing for acute cytokine-driven shock.
wrongExplanations.1: Plasma exchange is the treatment for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, removing an ADAMTS13 inhibitor and replacing the enzyme. It is not used for cytokine release syndrome, and there are no schistocytes or microangiopathic features here.
wrongExplanations.2: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells and would deplete B lymphocytes. The problem here is activated T CELLS and the cytokines they release, so a B-cell-directed antibody addresses neither the effector cell nor the mediator.
wrongExplanations.3: Heparin would be appropriate if this were a thrombotic complication. His picture is distributive shock with a hyperinflammatory profile, and anticoagulating a patient likely to be thrombocytopenic after this therapy would add bleeding risk with no benefit.

questions.eli5: His own T cells were re-engineered to hunt the leukemia, and when they found it they all switched on at once and flooded his body with inflammatory signals. The result looks exactly like severe sepsis, but the cultures are negative. A drug that blocks the main signal, interleukin-6, switches the storm off without killing the engineered cells.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with HIV infection has been taking tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz for 3 years with an undetectable viral load. He acknowledges that he ran out of medication and took none for 6 weeks. On restarting the same regimen, his plasma HIV RNA level remains 44,000 copies/mL after 12 weeks of documented adherence, and his CD4 count has fallen from 610 to 380/μL. Genotypic resistance testing identifies a single K103N substitution in the reverse transcriptase gene. Which of the following best explains why this single mutation caused failure of an entire drug class?
choices: A. All members of the class are competitive substrates at the enzyme's active site
B. All members of the class are prodrugs requiring the same activating enzyme
C. All members of the class bind the same allosteric pocket on reverse transcriptase
D. The mutation abolishes the proofreading function of the viral polymerase
E. The mutation prevents the drug from entering the cell
questions.explanation: The two reverse transcriptase inhibitor classes fail differently, and the reason is where each binds. NON-NUCLEOSIDE inhibitors (efavirenz, nevirapine, doravirine, rilpivirine) all dock into the SAME hydrophobic allosteric pocket adjacent to the active site, distorting the enzyme. Because every member depends on that one pocket, a single point mutation reshaping it — K103N being the classic — confers high-level resistance to essentially the WHOLE CLASS at once. This gives the class a notoriously LOW GENETIC BARRIER to resistance, which is why brief lapses in adherence are so costly. NUCLEOSIDE inhibitors sit at the opposite extreme: they are nucleoside ANALOGUES that bind competitively at the active site, so resistance mutations tend to REDUCE affinity rather than abolish it, and meaningful resistance generally requires ACCUMULATED mutations. Protease inhibitors are at the far end of the spectrum, where resistance is uncommon in patients not previously treated with one. His 6-week interruption on a regimen containing a low-barrier drug is exactly the setting in which such a mutation is selected.

wrongExplanations.0: This describes the NUCLEOSIDE inhibitors, which compete at the active site as nucleoside analogues — and it describes precisely why they behave the OPPOSITE way, generally requiring several accumulated mutations before resistance becomes clinically meaningful.
wrongExplanations.1: Tenofovir is a prodrug and the nucleoside analogues do require intracellular phosphorylation, but non-nucleoside inhibitors act directly without activation. A shared activating enzyme is not what links the class, and a reverse transcriptase mutation would not affect a host kinase anyway.
wrongExplanations.3: HIV reverse transcriptase has NO proofreading exonuclease activity to begin with. That is the reason for its high error rate and enormous viral diversity, which is why combination therapy is required — but it is a baseline property of the enzyme, not something a resistance mutation abolishes.
wrongExplanations.4: K103N is a substitution within the reverse transcriptase gene and alters the target enzyme inside the cell. It does not affect drug uptake, and these agents cross membranes freely.

questions.eli5: Every drug in this class works by wedging into the same small pocket on one viral enzyme. Change the shape of that pocket with a single mutation and none of them fit any more. Other HIV drug classes attach differently, so they need several mutations to stop working.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is seen 5 days after placement of a drug-eluting coronary stent for an acute coronary syndrome. He was discharged on aspirin 325 mg daily and ticagrelor. He comes to the office because of a 3-day history of shortness of breath that occurs at rest, comes on without exertion, and resolves spontaneously within minutes. He has no chest pain, orthopnea, cough, fever, or leg swelling. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 56/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Physical examination shows clear lung fields, no jugular venous distention, and no peripheral edema. An ECG shows sinus bradycardia with occasional ventricular pauses. A chest x-ray and D-dimer are normal, and troponin is not elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: A. Add furosemide for presumed decompensated heart failure
B. Begin empiric therapeutic anticoagulation for presumed pulmonary embolism
C. Discontinue ticagrelor and all antiplatelet therapy immediately
D. Perform CT pulmonary angiography to exclude pulmonary embolism
E. Reduce the aspirin dose to 81 mg daily and reassure him about the dyspnea
questions.explanation: Two ticagrelor-specific facts explain this entire visit. First, DYSPNEA is a well-recognized and generally benign adverse effect, occurring in roughly 10% to 15% of patients — it is typically at rest rather than exertional, transient, self-limited, and unaccompanied by hypoxemia or any abnormality on examination or imaging, exactly as here. Its mechanism relates to adenosine: ticagrelor inhibits adenosine reuptake, and adenosine stimulates pulmonary vagal afferents. The same adenosine effect explains his BRADYARRHYTHMIA and ventricular pauses, the second recognized adverse effect. Second, and this is the actionable error: maintenance ASPIRIN MUST BE KEPT AT OR BELOW 100 mg DAILY with ticagrelor, because higher doses paradoxically REDUCE its efficacy. He was discharged on 325 mg, which must be corrected to 81 mg. Recognizing the syndrome matters because the wrong response — stopping antiplatelet therapy days after stenting — risks stent thrombosis.

wrongExplanations.0: Heart failure would give exertional dyspnea with orthopnea, jugular venous distention, crackles, and edema. All are explicitly absent, his oxygen saturation is 98%, and diuresing a euvolemic patient would achieve nothing.
wrongExplanations.1: Empiric anticoagulation for pulmonary embolism is not justified with a normal D-dimer, normal oxygen saturation, no tachycardia, and no risk factors — and it would add bleeding risk in a patient already on dual antiplatelet therapy days after an acute coronary syndrome.
wrongExplanations.2: Stopping all antiplatelet therapy 5 days after drug-eluting stent placement is the most dangerous option available. Premature discontinuation is a leading cause of stent thrombosis, which carries high mortality. The dyspnea is benign; the response to it would not be.
wrongExplanations.3: CT pulmonary angiography would be reasonable if pretest probability were meaningful, but the normal D-dimer already makes pulmonary embolism very unlikely, and the syndrome fits a recognized drug effect. It would also expose a patient with normal renal function to unnecessary contrast and radiation.

questions.eli5: One of his new heart drugs is known to cause brief episodes of breathlessness at rest and a slow pulse, without anything actually wrong with the lungs — his oxygen and every test are normal. The important catch is that his aspirin dose is too high, which makes that same drug work less well. Stopping the drugs entirely would risk the stent clotting shut.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation has maintained a stable international normalized ratio between 2.2 and 2.6 for 2 years on 5 mg daily. He is seen in clinic 10 days after completing a course of an antibiotic for cellulitis. He reports bleeding gums and one episode of epistaxis. His diet has been poor for the past week because of the illness, and he says he has been eating far fewer salads than usual. He drinks no alcohol. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scattered ecchymoses over both forearms and dried blood at the nares; there is no active bleeding and no neurologic deficit. His international normalized ratio today is 6.8, and hemoglobin is 12.9 g/dL. Which of the following combinations of factors best explains the rise in his international normalized ratio?
choices: A. Decreased dietary vitamin K intake and induction of warfarin metabolism by the antibiotic
B. Decreased dietary vitamin K intake and inhibition of warfarin metabolism by the antibiotic
C. Increased dietary vitamin K intake and displacement of warfarin from albumin
D. Increased dietary vitamin K intake and inhibition of warfarin metabolism by the antibiotic
E. Reduced gastrointestinal absorption of warfarin and increased renal clearance
questions.explanation: Warfarin's international normalized ratio moves for pharmacoKINETIC and pharmacoDYNAMIC reasons, and both are operating here. PHARMACODYNAMIC: warfarin competes with vitamin K, so the effect of a fixed dose depends on how much vitamin K arrives. Green leafy vegetables are the major dietary source, and he has been eating far fewer — less competing substrate means MORE anticoagulant effect. Antibiotics compound this by killing the gut flora that synthesize vitamin K. PHARMACOKINETIC: warfarin is cleared by CYP2C9, and many antibiotics — metronidazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluconazole, and the macrolides — INHIBIT it, so warfarin accumulates. The two effects push in the SAME direction and together produce a dramatic rise. The underlying pharmacogenomics explain why patients differ so much at baseline: CYP2C9 variants slow metabolism, and VKORC1 variants alter sensitivity of the target enzyme itself. Management of an international normalized ratio of 6.8 without serious bleeding is to hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K; four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for serious or life-threatening hemorrhage.

wrongExplanations.0: Enzyme INDUCTION would accelerate warfarin clearance and LOWER the international normalized ratio, which is the opposite of what happened. Induction is the mechanism behind rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and St John's wort causing warfarin failure.
wrongExplanations.2: Increased vitamin K intake would supply more substrate to compete with warfarin and would REDUCE the international normalized ratio — the classic scenario of a patient who starts eating more salad and loses anticoagulation. He describes the opposite.
wrongExplanations.3: This combines a factor that would LOWER the ratio (more dietary vitamin K) with one that would raise it, and the vitamin K direction is wrong. Protein-binding displacement is also largely a theoretical mechanism that rarely produces clinically important warfarin interactions.
wrongExplanations.4: Warfarin is almost completely absorbed orally and is cleared by hepatic metabolism, not by the kidney. Increased renal clearance would in any case LOWER the drug level and the international normalized ratio.

questions.eli5: Warfarin works by competing with vitamin K, so anything that lowers vitamin K makes it stronger. He ate far fewer greens while ill, and the antibiotic both killed the gut bacteria that make vitamin K and slowed the liver enzyme that clears the drug. Three pushes in the same direction sent his level far too high.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-week history of a rapidly enlarging, painless mass in the right side of his neck, drenching night sweats, and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss. He has no history of serious illness. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a firm, fixed 9-cm right cervical mass and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy; the spleen is palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 10.4 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 8,600/mm3 with a normal differential, a platelet count of 210,000/mm3, and a lactate dehydrogenase of 1,460 U/L. Excisional biopsy of the cervical node shows diffuse effacement of architecture by sheets of large lymphoid cells with vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemistry is positive for CD20 and BCL6 and negative for CD3, CD5, and cyclin D1; the Ki-67 proliferation index is 78%. Which of the following best describes the expected response to treatment?
choices: A. An aggressive course that is almost never curable regardless of the therapy given
B. An aggressive course that is nonetheless curable in most patients with immunochemotherapy
C. An indolent course best managed by observation until symptoms or organ threat develop in the patient
D. An indolent course with repeated response and relapse and a low likelihood of cure
E. Cure by eradication of an underlying chronic bacterial infection
questions.explanation: Sheets of LARGE CD20-positive B cells with a Ki-67 of 78% is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma — the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma — and it illustrates the central paradox of lymphoma therapy. DIFFERENTIATION STAGE SETS THE TEMPO: less differentiated means aggressive, more differentiated means indolent. And that inverts CURABILITY, because chemotherapy kills DIVIDING cells. An aggressive lymphoma with a proliferation index approaching 80% has nearly its entire population in cycle at any moment, so cytotoxic therapy reaches almost all of it — hence cure in a majority with R-CHOP, despite death within months if untreated. An indolent lymphoma divides slowly, so most cells are never exposed to the drug's mechanism; it responds, relapses, and responds again over years without being cured. The corollary is the tumor lysis risk: the same rapid turnover that makes aggressive disease curable makes it dangerous to treat, so prophylaxis is given before the first cycle.

wrongExplanations.0: An aggressive but essentially incurable course would describe mantle cell lymphoma, where despite good initial responses essentially everyone relapses. Mantle cell is excluded here by immunophenotype: it is CD5-POSITIVE and expresses cyclin D1 from t(11;14), and both are negative in this biopsy.
wrongExplanations.2: Observation until symptoms develop is a legitimate strategy for asymptomatic low-burden FOLLICULAR lymphoma or early chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Applying it to a 9-cm mass growing over 3 weeks with B symptoms and a lactate dehydrogenase of 1,460 U/L would be fatal within months.
wrongExplanations.3: An indolent, relapsing, incurable course describes follicular lymphoma, which shows SMALL CLEAVED cells in a nodular pattern with t(14;18), CD10 and BCL2 positivity, and a LOW proliferation index. His cells are large and diffuse with a Ki-67 of 78%.
wrongExplanations.4: Cure by treating an underlying infection describes gastric MALT lymphoma responding to Helicobacter pylori eradication — a marginal zone lymphoma that remains antigen-dependent. That mechanism does not apply to a high-grade nodal large B-cell lymphoma.

questions.eli5: Cancer cells that divide fast are dangerous but also vulnerable, because chemotherapy kills cells while they are dividing. Nearly 80% of his tumor is actively dividing, so treatment reaches almost all of it and most patients are cured. Slow-growing lymphomas are the opposite — less alarming, but far harder to eliminate.

questions.stem:
A 54-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis is admitted with hematemesis from esophageal varices. Bleeding is controlled endoscopically. The intern proposes transfusing fresh frozen plasma to correct his coagulopathy before a planned paracentesis. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus, spider angiomata, ascites, and asterixis. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  9.4 g/dL
    Platelet count                              74,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            21 sec (N=11–14)
    International normalized ratio              1.9
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       41 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  188 mg/dL (N=200–400)
    D-dimer                                     Mildly increased
    Factor VIII activity                        168% (N=50–150)

Which of the following findings most strongly argues that this coagulopathy is due to hepatic synthetic failure rather than disseminated intravascular coagulation?
choices: A. The elevated factor VIII activity
B. The mildly increased D-dimer
C. The platelet count of 74,000/mm3
D. The prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time
E. The reduced fibrinogen concentration
questions.explanation: Liver disease and disseminated intravascular coagulation overlap almost completely on a routine coagulation screen — both prolong the prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, both lower fibrinogen, both drop the platelet count, and both can raise D-dimer. FACTOR VIII is what separates them, and the reason is anatomical: factor VIII is the ONE coagulation factor NOT made primarily by the hepatocyte — it is synthesized largely by endothelial cells. So in hepatic synthetic failure every other factor falls while factor VIII is PRESERVED, and it is often frankly ELEVATED, both as an acute-phase reactant and because von Willebrand factor rises and protects it. In disseminated intravascular coagulation, by contrast, factor VIII is CONSUMED along with everything else and falls. His value of 168% therefore points firmly to liver disease. The management point matters too: an international normalized ratio in cirrhosis does NOT reliably predict bleeding, because the liver also fails to make the natural anticoagulants proteins C and S — the system is rebalanced, not simply anticoagulated. Only about 30% factor activity is needed to clot, so transfusing plasma for an international normalized ratio of 1.9 before a low-risk procedure is volume and risk for no benefit.

wrongExplanations.1: A raised D-dimer is compatible with both. It rises in disseminated intravascular coagulation from fibrin turnover, but also in cirrhosis from reduced hepatic clearance of fibrin degradation products and from ascites. It cannot discriminate.
wrongExplanations.2: Thrombocytopenia occurs in both, and in cirrhosis it has its own explanations — splenic sequestration from portal hypertension and reduced hepatic thrombopoietin production. It is expected in either diagnosis and so distinguishes neither.
wrongExplanations.3: A prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time simply reflects deficiency of intrinsic and common pathway factors, which occurs in both conditions. It tells you factors are low without telling you why.
wrongExplanations.4: A low fibrinogen occurs in both — consumed in disseminated intravascular coagulation, and under-synthesized in advanced liver disease. A rapidly FALLING serial fibrinogen would favor consumption, but a single mildly reduced value does not discriminate.

questions.eli5: A failing liver and a consumption coagulopathy look nearly identical on the usual clotting tests. One clotting factor is made by blood vessel lining rather than by the liver, so it survives when the liver fails but gets used up when factors are being consumed. His level is high, which points at the liver.

questions.stem:
A 12-year-old boy with beta-thalassemia major has received transfusions every 3 to 4 weeks since the age of 2 years. He comes to the office for routine follow-up. He has been inconsistent with his oral medications for the past 2 years. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows generalized bronze-grey skin discoloration, a liver palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin, and Tanner stage 1 development at an age when stage 2 or 3 would be expected. Laboratory studies show:

    Serum ferritin              4,800 ng/mL
    Transferrin saturation      92%
    Alanine aminotransferase    112 U/L
    Fasting serum glucose       168 mg/dL

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging shows a shortened T2* consistent with myocardial iron loading, and the left ventricular ejection fraction is 48%. Which of the following best explains the underlying problem, and what is the appropriate treatment?
choices: A. Hemolysis of transfused erythrocytes releasing free heme into the plasma; treat with corticosteroids
B. Iron accumulation because humans have no regulated route for iron excretion; treat with a chelating agent
C. Iron accumulation from excessive dietary intake of iron; treat with strict dietary restriction
D. Iron accumulation from hepcidin excess trapping iron within macrophages; treat with regular phlebotomy
E. Secondary hemochromatosis from increased duodenal absorption alone; treat with regular phlebotomy
questions.explanation: Each unit of packed erythrocytes contains roughly 200 to 250 mg of iron, and a patient transfused monthly for a decade receives grams of it. The decisive physiologic fact is that humans have NO REGULATED MECHANISM FOR EXCRETING IRON — absorption is regulated, excretion is not. Iron that arrives in a transfusion therefore has nowhere to go, transferrin becomes saturated, and toxic non-transferrin-bound iron deposits in liver, heart, and endocrine organs. That explains his entire examination: bronze-grey skin, hepatomegaly with transaminitis, diabetes from pancreatic islet deposition, delayed puberty from pituitary and gonadal deposition, and — the finding that most threatens his life — myocardial loading with a falling ejection fraction, since cardiac disease is the leading cause of death in transfusion-dependent thalassemia. Because the iron cannot be excreted, it must be BOUND AND CARRIED OUT: chelation with deferasirox or deferiprone orally, or deferoxamine parenterally. Cardiac T2* magnetic resonance imaging guides intensity, because serum ferritin correlates poorly with myocardial loading. His inconsistent oral medication is the missed chelation.

wrongExplanations.0: Hemolysis of transfused cells does occur to some degree but does not cause this syndrome, and corticosteroids treat immune-mediated destruction. Nothing here suggests an immune process: he has no positive antiglobulin test, no acute hemoglobin drop, and the findings are those of chronic organ deposition.
wrongExplanations.2: Dietary iron is a trivial contributor compared with transfused iron, and restricting it cannot remove grams already deposited in his heart and liver. Dietary advice is a reasonable adjunct and nothing more.
wrongExplanations.3: This inverts the physiology. In thalassemia, ineffective erythropoiesis SUPPRESSES hepcidin, which increases duodenal absorption — the opposite of hepcidin excess. And phlebotomy is impossible in a patient who is transfusion-DEPENDENT and already anemic; removing his blood is precisely what he cannot tolerate.
wrongExplanations.4: Increased duodenal absorption does contribute in thalassemia, but it is far from the whole story in a monthly-transfused patient, where the transfusions dominate. The treatment named is the critical error: phlebotomy is the correct therapy for HEREDITARY hemochromatosis in a patient with normal hemoglobin, and is contraindicated here.

questions.eli5: Every bag of blood carries a load of iron, and the body has no way to get rid of extra iron — it can only control how much it takes in. After ten years of monthly transfusions it has piled up in his skin, liver, pancreas, and now his heart. A medicine that grabs the iron and carries it out in the urine or stool is the only way to remove it.

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate 24 mL/min/1.73 m2) is admitted with a gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Endoscopy shows a bleeding gastric ulcer, which is clipped successfully. Twelve hours later she continues to ooze from the ulcer base on repeat endoscopy and has diffuse bruising at venipuncture sites. She takes no anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs and has taken no nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 98/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  8.2 g/dL
    Platelet count                              214,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            12 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       32 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  318 mg/dL (N=200–400)
    Blood urea nitrogen                         98 mg/dL
    Serum creatinine                            6.2 mg/dL

A peripheral blood smear shows erythrocytes with numerous short, evenly spaced blunt spicules distributed regularly around the circumference. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her bleeding tendency?
choices: A. Cryoprecipitate
B. Desmopressin
C. Fresh frozen plasma
D. Platelet transfusion
E. Vitamin K
questions.explanation: Her platelet count and every clotting time are NORMAL, yet she is bleeding — which localizes the defect to platelet FUNCTION, something no routine coagulation assay can detect, since the platelets were spun out before the plasma assays began. Uremia impairs platelet adhesion and aggregation through accumulated guanidinosuccinic acid and other retained toxins, which interfere with von Willebrand factor-mediated adhesion and with platelet granule release. The smear supports the diagnosis: ECHINOCYTES (burr cells) have EVEN, regularly spaced spicules and point to uremia — remember that Echinocyte has Even spicules, while an ACanthocyte has Asymmetric ones and points to liver disease. Desmopressin is the treatment: it releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies, transiently improving adhesion within about an hour. Adjuncts include correcting the anemia (erythrocytes push platelets toward the vessel wall, so a hematocrit above roughly 30% improves hemostasis), cryoprecipitate, conjugated estrogens for a longer effect, and dialysis to remove the toxins.

wrongExplanations.0: Cryoprecipitate is a reasonable second-line option in uremic bleeding because it supplies von Willebrand factor multimers, but it is a pooled blood product with transfusion risk, and desmopressin achieves the same end faster and without exposure. Her fibrinogen of 318 mg/dL is normal, so the usual indication is absent.
wrongExplanations.2: Fresh frozen plasma replaces coagulation factors. Her prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen are all normal, so there are no factors to replace — the platelets are present but not working.
wrongExplanations.3: Platelet transfusion has little benefit here, and the reason is instructive: transfused platelets enter the same uremic plasma and are rapidly rendered dysfunctional by the same circulating toxins. Her count of 214,000/mm3 is normal, so there is no numerical deficit to correct.
wrongExplanations.4: Vitamin K corrects deficiency of factors II, VII, IX, and X, which would prolong the prothrombin time first. Her prothrombin time is 12 seconds and entirely normal.

questions.eli5: She has plenty of platelets and her clotting tests are normal, yet she keeps oozing — so the platelets are present but not sticking properly. Waste products that her failing kidneys cannot clear are coating them and blocking that stickiness. A drug that releases the body's own platelet glue from blood vessel walls restores it temporarily.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of abdominal pain, vomiting, and a rapidly enlarging abdomen for 10 days. He has had no fever. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a firm, irregular mass filling the right lower quadrant and extending across the midline, with no organomegaly and no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 10.6 g/dL, a leukocyte count of 9,200/mm3, a platelet count of 268,000/mm3, a lactate dehydrogenase of 3,900 U/L, and a uric acid of 9.8 mg/dL. Biopsy of the mass shows sheets of intermediate-sized lymphoid cells with numerous interspersed pale macrophages containing apoptotic debris. Immunohistochemistry is positive for CD20 and CD10 and negative for CD5 and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase; the Ki-67 proliferation index approaches 100%. Cytogenetic studies show t(8;14). Which of the following is the most important measure to institute BEFORE beginning chemotherapy?
choices: A. Aggressive hydration with a urate-lowering agent
B. Insertion of a central venous catheter for stem cell collection
C. Placement of a percutaneous nephrostomy
D. Prophylactic cranial irradiation
E. Transfusion to a hemoglobin concentration above 10 g/dL
questions.explanation: t(8;14) juxtaposes MYC to the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer, driving relentless proliferation — a Ki-67 approaching 100% means essentially EVERY cell is in cycle. That is Burkitt lymphoma, and the macrophages ingesting apoptotic debris among the tumor cells produce the classic starry-sky appearance. It has the shortest doubling time of any human tumor, and two consequences follow directly from that single fact. First, it is exquisitely chemosensitive and highly CURABLE, because cytotoxic therapy reaches virtually the whole population. Second — and this is the immediate danger — the same turnover makes it the highest-risk tumor for TUMOR LYSIS SYNDROME. His lactate dehydrogenase of 3,900 U/L and uric acid of 9.8 mg/dL show that cells are already lysing spontaneously before any treatment. Massive lysis on treatment releases potassium, phosphate, and urate, with calcium falling as it precipitates with phosphate, and urate crystals obstructing renal tubules. Prophylaxis before the first dose is therefore mandatory: vigorous hydration plus a urate-lowering agent — rasburicase in high-risk disease, with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status checked first, or allopurinol in lower-risk cases.

wrongExplanations.1: Autologous stem cell collection has no role in the primary treatment of Burkitt lymphoma, which is cured with intensive multi-agent chemotherapy. Collecting stem cells from a patient with circulating or marrow disease also risks reinfusing tumor.
wrongExplanations.2: Nephrostomy would be indicated for established obstructive uropathy from tumor compressing the ureters. There is no evidence of obstruction here, and it does not address the metabolic catastrophe that treatment is about to trigger.
wrongExplanations.3: Central nervous system prophylaxis IS important in Burkitt lymphoma, which has a high propensity for meningeal spread — but it is delivered as INTRATHECAL chemotherapy as part of the regimen, not as cranial irradiation, and it is not the measure that must precede the first dose.
wrongExplanations.4: Transfusion to an arbitrary hemoglobin target is not indicated; the restrictive threshold is 7 g/dL in a stable patient, and his hemoglobin is 10.6 g/dL. Transfusing also adds potassium and volume ahead of a lysis syndrome.

questions.eli5: This tumor doubles faster than any other, so nearly every cell is dividing at once. That makes chemotherapy remarkably effective — but it also means a huge number of cells will burst apart together and dump their contents into the blood, which can stop the kidneys and the heart. Fluids and a urate-lowering drug go in before the first dose.

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man comes to the office because of fatigue and abdominal discomfort for 4 months. He drinks no alcohol and takes no medications. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor and a spleen palpated 9 cm below the left costal margin. There is NO lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  8.8 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  27%
    Leukocyte count             1,900/mm3
      Segmented neutrophils     18%
    Platelet count              62,000/mm3
    Reticulocyte count          1.1%

Repeated attempts at bone marrow aspiration yield no material. A core biopsy specimen shows a diffuse interstitial infiltrate of small lymphoid cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and fine circumferential cytoplasmic projections, surrounded by a network of reticulin fibers. Flow cytometry shows a monoclonal B-cell population expressing CD19, CD20, CD11c, CD25, and CD103. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Aplastic anemia
B. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
C. Hairy cell leukemia
D. Mantle cell lymphoma
E. Primary myelofibrosis
questions.explanation: Three findings converge. The IMMUNOPHENOTYPE is decisive: CD11c, CD25, and CD103 co-expressed on a monoclonal B-cell population is the diagnostic triad of hairy cell leukemia (BRAF V600E mutation is present in nearly all cases and is confirmatory). The MORPHOLOGY matches — small lymphoid cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and fine circumferential projections, the 'hairy' cells that name the disease. And the CLINICAL PATTERN is characteristic and deliberately paradoxical: massive SPLENOMEGALY with PANCYTOPENIA but NO LYMPHADENOPATHY, which is unusual for a lymphoid neoplasm and is one of the most useful discriminators. The DRY TAP is expected — the infiltrate induces reticulin fibrosis, so aspiration fails and a core biopsy is mandatory, exactly as happened here. Note that a dry tap has a short differential: hairy cell leukemia, primary myelofibrosis, and marrow packed by any infiltrate. Treatment with a purine analogue, cladribine or pentostatin, produces durable remissions in the great majority.

wrongExplanations.0: Aplastic anemia also causes pancytopenia with a low reticulocyte count, but the marrow is HYPOCELLULAR — mostly fat, with no infiltrate and no fibrosis — and it aspirates readily. Aplastic anemia also causes no splenomegaly, whereas his spleen extends 9 cm below the costal margin.
wrongExplanations.1: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is the other common mature B-cell neoplasm of this age group, but it presents with a LYMPHOCYTOSIS, often marked, with generalized LYMPHADENOPATHY and smudge cells. Its phenotype is CD5 and CD23 positive — neither is expressed here — and he is lymphopenic rather than lymphocytotic.
wrongExplanations.3: Mantle cell lymphoma is CD5-POSITIVE and expresses cyclin D1 from t(11;14), and it typically presents with widespread lymphadenopathy and often gastrointestinal involvement. Neither the phenotype nor the absence of nodes fits.
wrongExplanations.4: Primary myelofibrosis is the strongest competitor: it also gives massive splenomegaly, cytopenias, a dry tap, and marrow fibrosis. It is separated by two things — its smear shows a LEUKOERYTHROBLASTIC picture with teardrop cells and nucleated erythrocytes, and its marrow shows clusters of atypical MEGAKARYOCYTES with a JAK2 mutation, not a monoclonal B-cell infiltrate with this surface phenotype.

questions.eli5: His spleen is enormous and all three blood counts are low, yet his lymph nodes are completely normal — an unusual combination that narrows things down fast. The marrow could not be sucked out because the cancer cells provoke scar fibers, so a core of bone was taken instead. The cells have fine hair-like projections and a specific trio of surface markers that name the disease.
